name: Battle of the Teutoburg Forest
info: An alliance of Germanic peoples led by Arminius ambushed three Roman legions under Publius Quinctilius Varus in 9 CE, possibly near Kalkriese, and ended Roman expansion beyond the Rhine.

facts.place: Possibly near Kalkriese, north of Osnabrück in Lower Saxony, Germany; the site was long unidentified and the older theories placed it elsewhere
facts.sides: The Roman Empire under the governor Publius Quinctilius Varus, with three legions (about 15,000 men) and nine small auxiliary units (about 4,500 men), though estimates of his army generally range from 20,000 to 30,000; an alliance of Germanic peoples under Arminius of the Cherusci, whose numbers are a guess: Murdoch suggests 25,000, Wells 17,000 to 100,000, Delbrück 20,000 to 30,000
facts.outcome: The Roman army was ambushed and destroyed over several days and Varus killed himself. Rome lost its forts east of the Rhine, and the Rhine became the frontier.

t: Arminius was born into the Cherusci, was taken to Rome as a hostage, received a Roman education, joined the Roman cavalry and commanded auxiliaries, so he knew how the Romans fought and was trusted by Varus.

The Roman column was strung out over 15 to 20 kilometres of forest and then caught on a strip of ground only about 100 metres wide between a hill and a bog, in front of a wall the Germanic warriors had built.
After the defeat the legion numbers XVII, XVIII and XIX were not used again, and later Roman campaigns under Germanicus recovered two of the three lost eagles in 14 and 15 CE and the third in 41 CE.
dyk: Varus's army was paid on the morning of 7 September, and the large number of coins handed out became an archaeological marker: Tony Clunn's metal detector found coins of Augustus's reign at Kalkriese in 1987.
ev: Drusus defeats the Cherusci, and the boy Arminius is taken to Rome as a hostage
Varus takes command of the legions in Germania
Varus leaves winter quarters and sets up a summer camp, probably near Minden, in Cherusci lands
The army moves out for a campaign against the Angrivarii, and Arminius leaves it
The Germanic alliance attacks the army in the forest and at Kalkriese, and Varus kills himself
The fort of Aliso holds out for weeks before its garrison breaks through to the Rhine
Germanicus campaigns east of the Rhine and recovers two of the lost eagles
Arminius is poisoned by fellow Germans

sections.background:
Julius Caesar twice crossed the Rhine in the Gallic Wars (58 to 50 BCE), but the engagements were inconclusive. After Augustus reorganised Gaul into three provinces, policy towards the Germanic lands remains unclear. One theory holds that he meant the Rhine to be the northern border, another that the border was fluid and the troops were there to keep order. The Lollian disaster of 16 BCE led to a reorganisation of the legions, and Drusus campaigned against the Germans from 11 to 9 BCE until he died in a riding accident. Tiberius took command in 8 BCE, and Lucius Domitius Ahenobarbus later crossed the Elbe, the first and last Roman general to do so.

By the turn of the century the Romans felt secure, reassured by cross-border trade and relative peace. In early 6 CE a huge army of 13 legions and about 100,000 men set out against Maroboduus, king of the Marcomanni, a tribe of the Suebi. Tiberius had to break off when the Great Illyrian Revolt began in the Balkans. He recognised Maroboduus as king and sent eight legions to crush the rebellion, which lasted nearly four years. Only three legions remained to face the Germanic tribesmen, and the weakened Roman position gave an opportunity for a Germanic rebellion.
sections.forces:
Publius Quinctilius Varus had been quaestor in 22 BCE, governor of Africa in 8 BCE and of Syria in 7 BCE, and had married the emperor's great-niece. Michael McNally assesses that he was sent to Germania in 7 CE for his political skill, to deal with factionalism among the tribes, not for his military ability. His ruthlessness, including crucifixion of insurgents, was known beyond the empire. He had five legions, of which three were with him at the battle, about 15,000 men, with nine small auxiliary units of about 4,500. How many men were truly under his command is unclear, and estimates generally range from 20,000 to 30,000. McNally puts the likely number of combatants at 17,000 and the civilians at a few hundred.

Arminius was a nobleman of the Cherusci, taken hostage when Drusus defeated his tribe in 8 BCE, when he was about ten. He was educated in Rome, joined the cavalry, commanded auxiliaries and was serving in Pannonia by 4 CE. On his return he became a trusted adviser to Varus while building an alliance of peoples that had been enemies, probably including the Cherusci, Marsi, Chatti and Bructeri. No Germanic records survive, so the size of his force is a guess: Adrian Murdoch suggests 25,000, Peter Wells gives estimates from 17,000 to 100,000 with 18,000 at the final stage, and Hans Delbrück 20,000 to 30,000. Most of the warriors had no armour and fought with a shield and a hunting spear or axe.
sections.course:
The Romans left their winter camps in March and planned a summer camp in Cherusci lands, probably near Minden. In July Arminius had allies raid the Romans and advised Varus to detach troops to put down unrest, which split his force. His father-in-law Segestes warned Varus of the treachery, but Varus disbelieved him. In late summer, on the way back to the Rhine, Varus heard of a rebellion that Arminius had invented. Arminius proposed a shorter route through the land of the Angrivarii, and on the morning of 7 September the army moved out. That evening Arminius left to gather his troops, taking a quarter of the Roman strength with him.

On 8 September the Bructeri attacked along a column stretched over 15 to 20 kilometres in thick forest, then withdrew. A downpour followed and Varus had a camp built. The Romans then marched by night into a second trap at the foot of Kalkriese Hill, where a gap of about 100 metres lay between the woods and the edge of the Great Bog, closed by a trench and an earthen wall from which the Germanic warriors attacked. The Romans failed to storm the wall. The legate Numonius Vala rode off with the cavalry and was overtaken and killed. Varus killed himself, the prefect Ceionius surrendered and later took his own life, and Eggius died leading his men.
sections.aftermath:
Roman casualties have been estimated at 15,000 to 20,000 dead, and many officers are said to have killed themselves. According to Tacitus, many officers were sacrificed in Germanic religious ceremonies. Others were ransomed, and some common soldiers appear to have been enslaved. Finds at Kalkriese suggest few Germanic losses, though the victors would probably have removed their own dead and buried their battle gear with them.

The Germanic alliance swept away the Roman forts and garrisons east of the Rhine. The fort of Aliso, most likely at Haltern am See, held out for many weeks, perhaps a few months, before the garrison under Lucius Caedicius and survivors of the battle broke through to the Rhine. This gave Lucius Nonius Asprenas time to organise the defence of the Rhine with two legions, and Tiberius arrived with a new army, so Arminius could not cross into Gaul.

According to Suetonius, Augustus was so shaken that he butted his head against the walls of his palace, shouting for his legions back. The numbers XVII, XVIII and XIX were never used again. Arminius sent Varus's head to Maroboduus with the offer of an alliance, but Maroboduus declined, sent the head to Rome for burial and stayed neutral. Tiberius took effective control and sent three legions to the Rhine to replace the lost ones.
sections.sources:
The Roman accounts stress the completeness of the defeat. Velleius Paterculus is the only contemporary chronicler to describe the summer, and McNally notes that he had reason to dislike Varus and that later accounts relied on him and took on his bias. Josephus, writing some decades afterwards, took a positive view of Varus, while Paterculus implicitly accuses him of corruption. Suetonius tells of Augustus's grief, Tacitus of the sacrifices and of the later burial of the bones, and Cassius Dio, who wrote in the Severan era, says that Varus was carrying out the later stages of colonising a German province.

For almost 2,000 years the site was unidentified. Several hundred theories followed the rediscovery of Tacitus in the 16th century, and in 1966 Harald Petrikovits grouped them into four: a northern theory, a Lippe theory, a Münsterland theory and a southern theory. In the 19th century the ridge called the Osning near Bielefeld was renamed the Teutoburg Forest. In 1987 Tony Clunn found coins from the reign of Augustus, none later, and lead sling bolts at Kalkriese, a site Theodor Mommsen had suggested. Excavations have found battle debris along a corridor almost 24 kilometres long and little more than 1.6 wide, a long wall of peat turves and sand, human remains and coins countermarked VAR. Kalkriese is now perceived to be an event of the battle. Of some 6,000 pieces of Roman equipment, only one item is clearly Germanic, a spur, which may reflect burial customs and perishable gear.
sections.legacy:
The battle is considered one of the most important defeats in Roman history. It ended the period of expansion under Augustus and dissuaded the Romans from conquering Germania. Germanicus campaigned in 14 to 16 CE, took Mattium, captured Arminius's wife Thusnelda and fought Arminius at the pontes longi and at Idistaviso and the Angrivarian Wall. Tiberius then halted the campaigns. Tacitus claims jealousy of Germanicus lay behind this, and that another summer would have ended the war. Arminius continued to fight, but the conflict remained a stalemate. He was poisoned in 21 CE by fellow Germans, possibly his own family, who feared his autocracy.

Some scholars have tempered the view that the defeat alone halted Roman expansion at the Rhine. The Rhine could be supplied from the Mediterranean by river, the region beyond had few villages, little food surplus and a lesser capacity for tribute, and in a cost-benefit analysis the prestige of conquest was outweighed by its cost. The provinces of Germania Inferior and Germania Superior were formally established in 85 CE.

From the rediscovery of the Roman sources in the 15th century the battle was given great weight, and Arminius, called Hermann, became a nationalist symbol. The Hermannsdenkmal near Detmold was begun in 1841 and finished in 1875, after the Franco-Prussian War. Handel's opera Arminio (1736) and Kleist's drama Die Hermannsschlacht (1808) treat the story.

summary: In September 9 CE an alliance of Germanic peoples under Arminius, a former Roman officer, ambushed and destroyed three Roman legions led by Varus, possibly near Kalkriese. Rome lost its forts east of the Rhine, and campaigns under Germanicus did not restore them.
references: Peter S. Wells, The Battle That Stopped Rome: Emperor Augustus, Arminius, and the Slaughter of the Legions in the Teutoburg Forest (W.W. Norton & Company, 2003)
Adrian Murdoch, Rome's Greatest Defeat: Massacre in the Teutoburg Forest (The History Press, 2012)
Michael McNally, Teutoburg Forest, AD 9: the destruction of Varus and his legions (Osprey Publishing, 2011)
notes: Date: the lead says 8 to 11 September; the body has the muster on 7 September, the first attack on 8 September, and the Kalkriese fighting after a night march; the article gives no dates for 9 to 11 September.

Site: the lead says 'possibly near modern Kalkriese'; the article says Kalkriese 'is now perceived to be an event of the Battle', so I kept the hedge. The article calls the Kalkriese corridor almost 24 km long, which is wider than the 100 m gap at the hill; both are given.

Self-contradiction: the article says Varus 'initially commanded five legions' (about 25,000) but only three were at the battle; I gave the three-legion figure and the 20,000 to 30,000 range as the article does. Its sentence that the loss of Arminius 'cut the size of the Roman army by a quarter' is used as written.
The article says Tiberius sent legions II Augusta, XX Valeria Victrix and XIII Gemina; I wrote 'three legions' only. It also says the third eagle was recovered in 41 CE by Publius Gabinius.

The article gives 'Bructeri' and 'Bructerii', 'Cherusci' and 'Cheruscii' variously; I used Bructeri and Cherusci. It says Arminius went north to gather the Angrivarii and Bructeri, and the Angrivarii lay in ambush at Kalkriese.

Left out: Petrikovits's four theories' detail, the later Harzhorn and Marcomannic Wars material, client kings, the popular-culture list beyond two works, Varus's Syrian career in detail, the Waldgirmes forum (mentioned only through Cassius Dio).
The article's 'Roman historians' Latin name for the battle (Clades Variana) is not used in the text.
'Hermann' is called in the article a mistranslation of 'Armin'; left out as a contested aside.
